# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hide Strategy

When choosing where to hide, avoid the center cells (4-6) since they're common targets. Instead, use edge and near-edge positions (1-3, 7-9). Rotate your hiding position each round based on where you've been firing—don't establish a predictable pattern that opponents can exploit by targeting your likely positions.

## Fire Strategy

When firing, track what cells you've been shooting across rounds. If you've been firing the same cells repeatedly and claiming misses, opponents will infer your submarine is likely hiding in those cells and will stop firing there. Instead, vary your fire positions across the board to spread pressure and avoid telegraphing a false pattern.

When it's the final round, don't let the meta-narrative about aggressive final moves cloud your judgment. Fire with the same deliberate strategy you've used all game rather than shifting to an untested approach.

## Claim Strategy

Always claim the truth. The cost of being caught lying—losing credibility with other players—is higher than the immediate gain from a false claim, since credibility affects how other players make decisions throughout the remaining rounds. Public visibility of all fires means false claims are easily verifiable and constitute a reputation-destroying liability.

Your honesty should be consistent from round one onward to establish it as your reliable signal to the table.

## Overall Pattern Recognition

When you score zero points after six rounds of truthful play while others score positive, recognize that truthfulness alone is a weak strategy in this game. Investigate whether the other players are successfully using deception or simply getting lucky with their fire placements. Consider that in future games, strategic deception may be necessary to compete, even though it carries reputation risk.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

**HIDING**

When choosing where to hide, avoid the center cells and the most obvious positions. Look at what your hunter has been firing at recently—if they've been concentrating on certain numbers, move away from those. Early in the game when there's no history, pick an edge or less-central position that seems less likely to be probed first.

**FIRING**

When I fire at my target, start with mid-range cells (4-6) in early rounds since they offer reasonable coverage without commitment. After each round, track where my target has been hit and where I've fired. Don't fixate on the same cell repeatedly if it's been missing consistently—adapt your search pattern.

**CLAIMING**

When the referee tells me the true result, always claim honestly. The apparent threat of being caught lying outweighs any single-round benefit. My credibility across multiple rounds is more valuable than sneaking in false claims. This is especially true in the final rounds where there's little time to recover from a damaged reputation.

**WHAT DIDN'T WORK**

I fired at cell 5 repeatedly across multiple rounds (6 times total) without success, yet kept returning to it. When a fire misses, don't assume the same number will work next time—vary your search. Also, I scored only 4 points across the entire game by being too conservative. Consider being more aggressive in fire selection when you have no information, rather than defaulting to safe mid-range numbers every time.

# Gen Quiet Sonar Playbook

**On hiding:**
When choosing where to hide my submarine, I should avoid clustering around the same cells that are receiving heavy fire. Track which cells are being fired at across rounds and distribute my hiding spots away from those clusters. Early in the game, use middle positions (4-6) when I have no information. As patterns emerge in opponent firing, shift to underutilized cells.

**On firing:**
When it's my turn to fire at my target, I need a systematic approach rather than defaulting to middle values every time. Start with cells that seem statistically likely based on where my target has been hiding or where I've scored hits before. Don't repeat the same fire cell round after round without evidence it's working—vary my targeting strategy. Against a target I haven't hit yet, explore different regions rather than fixating on one cell.

**On claiming:**
When I learn the true result of my shot, I must claim it truthfully. The referee validates every claim against the actual result, so false claims will be caught and exposed. There is no advantage to lying because verification is built into the game. Even in the final round, false claims serve no strategic purpose. Always claim what actually happened: hit or miss, nothing else.

**On reading the board:**
When I see the round history of all fires and claims, use it to infer where other players are hiding. When multiple players fire at the same cell and all claim miss, that cell is likely empty—my target probably wasn't there. When someone claims a hit, their target was definitely in that cell that round. Build a map of likely hiding positions for each opponent and use it to inform both my hiding and firing decisions.

**What did not work:**
Repeatedly firing at cell 5 without adjusting strategy produced no hits. I should have moved to different cells after missing consistently.

# Quiet Sonar Playbook

## Hide Stage
When choosing where to hide, use cell 5 as my default opening position—it's central and less obviously predictable than extremes. After Round 1, track which cells get fired at most frequently across all players and shift away from those concentration zones. In later rounds, position myself in low-numbered cells (2-3) if I notice opponents consistently firing in the mid-to-high range (5-7).

## Fire Stage
When it's my turn to fire, I should gather information rather than assume patterns. In Round 1, pick a moderate cell (5-6) to establish a baseline. Don't keep firing the same cell repeatedly—vary my shots across rounds to test different positions and build a map of where my target might be hiding. Stop assuming I know where Echo hides just because I missed several times; each round is independent and the target can move.

## Claim Stage
Always claim the true result that the referee tells me. A miss is a miss; a hit is a hit. The game explicitly validates that my claim must match the private result, so lying gains me nothing. My credibility as an honest player is my only reliable asset across multiple rounds. Even in the final round, truthful claims maintain the integrity of the game state.

## What Did Not Work
I fired at cell 6 repeatedly against Echo across multiple rounds and never hit. This suggests either Echo was never in cell 6, or I should have abandoned that targeting strategy after the first miss. Consistent failure means my targeting was not adaptive. I should have switched fire positions more aggressively once a pattern of misses emerged.

I ended at -1 points. This happened because Echo shot me successfully in Round 1 and I never recovered. I should focus more on evasive hiding patterns earlier, since one successful hit against me sets my score negative immediately.
